source_refs.note: The Knee-Jerk Reflex: a main subheading of 15.2.3 Reflex Arc, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 29-30.

blocks.text: Knee-jerk is a reflex that occurs when someone hits the tendon below the knee (the patellar tendon) with a hammer. Tapping on that tendon acts as a stimulus. This stimulus (tapping) is sensed by a receptor present in the quadriceps muscle of thigh. The receptor generates a nerve impulse in a sensory neuron. The sensory neuron carries this impulse travels to spinal cord. Here, the sensory neuron transfers the impulse to a motor neuron without involving an inter-neuron. The motor neuron carries the impulse to the effector (quadriceps muscle) which contracts. It leads to extension of the lower leg at the knee (i.e., the lower leg kicks forward).

blocks.alt: Side view of a bent leg. A hammer strikes the tendon below the knee. A sensory neuron runs from a receptor in the quadriceps muscle at the front of the thigh to the spinal cord, shown in cross-section. Inside the cord an interneuron is drawn, and two motor neurons leave the cord, one to the quadriceps and one to the hamstrings muscle at the back of the thigh.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.3: Knee-jerk reflex (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.3).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Spinal cord, Sensory neuron, Quadriceps muscle, Receptor, Hammer, Tendon, Hamstrings muscle, Interneuron, Motor neurons.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 15.3 labels 'Tnedon'; the correct spelling is Tendon, as drawn above.

In the meantime, sensory neuron also activates an inter-neuron in spinal cord. The inter-neuron releases chemicals which inhibit the motor neurons that connect to the hamstrings muscle. It results in the relaxation of hamstrings during the extension of the lower leg.
